speaker: Patient
text: 17-year-old female. The patient presents with a 5-day history of severe abdominal pain and cramping, accompanied by nausea and vomiting. She reports pain with urination and also experienced burning pain during sexual intercourse 3 days ago. She mentions being sexually active with one male partner, using condoms inconsistently.

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID) secondary to a sexually transmitted infection. The patient is a 17-year-old female with severe lower abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, dysuria, and a history of dyspareunia (painful intercourse). Her risk factors include inconsistent condom use and a new sexual partner. These findings are highly suggestive of ascending infection (likely chlamydia or gonorrhea) causing PID, rather than a simple urinary tract infection or appendicitis. I am confident in this diagnosis based on the classic presentation of pelvic pain, dyspareunia, and risk factors for STIs. No further tests are required for the diagnosis, though empiric treatment and partner notification are indicated.
